newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Politicians woo but women undecided.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Politicians woo but women undecided.

text.p: Grey, bespectacled and stolid, British Prime Minister John Major is a big hit with women.
Young, dashing and bright, his rival Tony Blair is not.
Blair's opposition Labour Party is far ahead in opinion polls, it has drastically raised women's profile in politics and Blair is patently a "new man", married to a highly successful woman.
Major's Conservative Party resembles a stuffy gentlemen's club. Cartoonists routinely portray Major as a spoof Superman, wearing y-fronts over his trousers.
So why is Blair regarded with suspicion by many female voters ahead of the May 1 election?
"British women historically vote Conservative and Labour is spending an awful lot of time trying to work out exactly why," said political scientist Dr Helen Margetts.
"None of the possible reasons are very attractive to feminists but one thing is sure: if women had voted the same way as men did in the last election, the Conservatives would not have won."
Political scientist Joni Lovenduski goes still further.
"If women had not had the vote, there would have been no Conservative governments between 1945 and 1979," she said. "Just imagine what a different place this would be."
In 1992, the Conservatives won their fourth election in a row since 1979 when Margaret Thatcher became Britain's first woman prime minister.
Labour says the so-called gender gap that lost it so many elections has largely closed, as young women warm to "New Labour" and older women, too, turn away from the Conservatives.
Yet pollsters found a consistent lag, sometimes as high as 22 points, when women and men were asked throughout last year if they were satisfied with the way Blair was doing his job.
Ask the same question about "grey man" Major and the women consistently polled more favourably than the men.
Women, it seems, don't quite trust the Labour leader.
CONTRADICTIONS

"On the surface there are contradictions. For instance, one in four women think Blair is smarmy compared to 15 percent for Major. Major comes across as more sincere although both men are perceived as equally capable," said Cara Lavan of MORI polling.
Blair is not the only problem. Alienated by Labour's macho, trade-union roots, women of a certain age have long toiled happily and hard in local Conservative politics.
To this day, the blue-rinsed brigade merrily stuff envelopes and run raffles, all the while urging tougher policies from politicians and the winsome wives by their side.
The men in charge have no choice but to listen: these women could decide the election.

For all the parties' nebulous efforts to pinpoint just what it is that women want, some facts are stark. There are more women voters than men. Since 1979, turnout among women has been higher than among men. Women form the majority of floating voters.
About one quarter of women have not yet decided how they will vote in the election compared with 16 percent of men, according to an analysis by the Demos think-tank.
"As the election approaches, politicians are finally waking up to the fact that winning women's votes could be the key to success at the polls. This is true for all parties," it said.

It said the Conservatives had squandered their natural advantage among women -- 12 percent of women who voted for them in 1992 have not decided how to vote this time -- and have even alientated their bedrock supporters in the over-55 age group with a series of u-turns and their perceived ineptitude.
Labour, while popular with young women, knows they often don't bother to vote on the day and, more worryingly, less than 20 percent of women say they trust Blair.

Some say it's his hair style (too coiffed), or his smile (insincere), others point to a dictatorial style of party management (Blair was briefly nicknamed Stalin), a coolness of manner and a stiffening of the party's social policy.

"It's this smoothy, synthetic, pop-star image that all the boys around him like but women don't. By making him so glitzy, they have damaged his sincerity," one female Labour member of parliament told the Independent on Sunday.
A top Conservative source concurred, saying: "Women are afraid that the whole of Tony Blair's New Labour is a rather corny chat-up line...I would tell him not to smile."
GENDER GAP NARROWING

The gender gap at the last election was six percentage points as the Conservatives had a four-point lead among men and a 10-point lead among women. While that gap has narrowed, according to recent polls, Blair's own popularity with women has fallen just as his standing among male voters has risen.
Analysts point to a host of reasons for the discrepancy, some driven by the party's programme, others by sheer style.
"All the evidence suggests that it is policies rather than hair-dos which influence women's voting decisions," said analyst Lovenduski, who decried male efforts to woo women with fluff.
Blair has worked hard on women as part of his plan to update the party. Gone are the smoke-filled rooms, the beery talk of worker solidarity and deep disdain for all things modern.
Instead, Blair has turned the Labour Party into a sleek new fighting force, loosening ties with the unions, stealing the centre ground and elevating a record number of women to positions of power.

According to an analysis in the Guardian newspaper, almost a quarter of Labour members of parliament will be women if Blair wins a sweeping majority. There could be 87 women Labour MPs compared with only 15 on the Conservative benches, it said.
But the mother of parliaments will remain overwhelmingly male. Conservative or Labour, women MPs often say they have more in common with each other than with men from their own parties.
MP Clare Short, one of Labour's most popular figures, was even more disparaging about men behaving badly at Westminster.
"Sometimes I feel embarrassed to be there. I hope my Mum isn't watching," she said of the sexist sneers, chants and relentless barracking that often passes for politics.
